query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled severe plastic deformation process (e.g., high‐strain‐rate cold rolling or equal channel angular pressing) followed by a precisely tuned annealing treatment will generate a nanostructured, twin‐rich BCC microstructure in equal-atomic NbMoTaW, thereby activating more slip systems at room temperature to improve ductility without degrading its high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical performance or its irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with excellent high-temperature properties and irradiation resistance (as predicted) but exhibiting very poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.intervention: Implement a severe plastic deformation process (via high-strain-rate cold rolling or equal channel angular pressing) followed by an optimized annealing treatment designed to refine the grain size and promote the formation of twin boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing for ductility, high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical testing, and irradiation assessments under service-relevant dose and flux conditions; processing parameters must be controlled to avoid the formation of secondary phases or compositional shifts.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanostructured BCC microstructure with a significantly increased twin boundary density and refined grain size.
generation.mechanism: Severe plastic deformation refines the microstructure and, when followed by controlled annealing, promotes twin-boundary formation. The twins act as additional barriers and sources for dislocation activity and provide extra slip systems at room temperature, thereby enhancing ductility while preserving the underlying high-melting, solid-solution characteristics that afford high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the processed alloy is expected to show a significant improvement in room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased plastic strain), while maintaining its excellent high-temperature mechanical strength at 1600 °C and its irradiation resistance remains comparable.
generation.baseline: Untreated equal-atomic NbMoTaW characterized by a coarse, single-phase BCC microstructure with poor room-temperature ductility yet excellent high-temperature mechanical performance and predicted irradiation resistance.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when the processing conditions (deformation and annealing) are carefully tuned to avoid triggering unwanted secondary phase formation or compositional segregation. The expected improvements are valid for testing temperatures up to 1600 °C and under irradiation conditions representative of service environments.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in precisely controlling the twin density and grain refinement without inadvertently promoting secondary phase precipitation; slight variations in processing parameters might also affect the uniformity of the twin distribution and, consequently, the ductility and high-temperature performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equal-atomic NbMoTaW samples. Set A undergoes the severe plastic deformation (using high-strain-rate cold rolling or ECAP) followed by the precisely tuned annealing treatment, and Set B serves as the untreated control. Use TEM and XRD to quantitatively assess grain size and twin-boundary density. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to evaluate ductility, high-temperature (1600 °C) mechanical tests (e.g., yield strength and creep resistance measurements), and standardized irradiation experiments (such as ion irradiation followed by defect analysis).
measurements: Grain size and twin boundary density (via TEM/XRD)
High-temperature mechanical properties at 1600 °C (yield strength, creep behavior)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed NbMoTaW samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in room-temperature ductility (i.e., improved plastic strain) while maintaining high-temperature mechanical performance (within experimental error relative to the untreated baseline) and comparable irradiation resistance, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. decision.trend: The early studies on refractory HEAs focused on demonstrating excellent high‐temperature strength and provided initial insights into ductility limitations. Early work (PMC4510962) showed that nanoscale architectures (e.g., thin-film pillars with strongly textured, columnar, nanometer‐sized grains) could significantly enhance ductility in small-scale tests, albeit not in bulk. Later work (PMC5995863) introduced a microstructural engineering concept – an ‘inverted’ microstructure, with discrete secondary B2 precipitates within a continuous BCC matrix – to improve room‐temperature ductility while maintaining high yield strength. Most recently (PMC10894205) investigations on the interplay of phase stability, dislocation behavior, and elemental contributions have provided a deeper understanding of the intrinsic factors that cause brittleness versus ductility in similar alloys. Thus, the evolution has been from computational predictions of irradiation resistance and demonstration of high‐temperature performance, to microstructural design strategies aimed at leveraging processing routes to overcome room‐temperature brittleness without sacrificing the high-temperature capability.
decision.unsolved: For equal-atomic NbMoTaW, the challenge remains how to activate additional ductile deformation mechanisms (such as slip system activation and, ideally, twin formation) at room temperature while preserving the high melting point, solid-solution stability, and irradiation resistance that are inherent to the pristine composition. In other words, a bulk processing route that tailors the microstructure to improve room-temperature ductility without triggering secondary phases or changes that would compromise high-temperature performance and radiation tolerance has not yet been demonstrated.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-strain-rate cold rolling or equal channel angular pressing) followed by a precisely tuned annealing treatment to induce a nanostructured, twin-rich microstructure in bulk NbMoTaW.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend seen in earlier works where reducing grain size and introducing twin boundaries (or inverting the usual microstructure) substantially improved room-temperature ductility in refractory HEAs. By using processing rather than composition modification, the intrinsic high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation resistance predicted for NbMoTaW are preserved, addressing the dual constraint posed in the research question.
